subtype: Why the scammer builds a persona [Observer]
passage:
It was Gargi's fourth visit to the Aizawl branch that month, and Lalremsiami, at the counter, recognised the account number on the transfer slip before she looked up.
"Same beneficiary?" she asked.
Gargi nodded, cheeks pink. "His business account is frozen. It's just until Friday."
Lalremsiami didn't scold. She lowered her voice. "Can I ask a few things, just between us? Have you met him in person?"
"Not yet. He's in Malta."
"Has he ever video called?"
"His camera..." Gargi trailed off.
Lalremsiami had seen this story in the bank's fraud training: the same charming engineer, the same frozen account, scripts shared by organised groups who do this all day. Gargi wasn't foolish. Gargi was up against professionals.
"Would you sit with our fraud officer for ten minutes before sending? No pressure. I'll come too."
Gargi looked at the slip for a long moment, then nodded.

qa.q: How many times had Gargi visited the branch that month?
qa.a: It was Gargi's fourth visit to the branch that month.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she recognised the account number?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt concerned but careful, wanting to protect Gargi without shaming her, which shows in her lowered voice and her choice not to scold.
Instead of scolding, Lalremsiami asked gentle private questions and offered to go with Gargi to the fraud officer, which kept Gargi from feeling ashamed and defensive.

qa.q: How might Gargi see things after the talk with the fraud officer?
qa.a: Gargi may feel hurt and embarrassed, but learning that organised groups run these scripts could ease the self-blame.

grounding: A bank counter worker notices repeated transfers to someone Gargi has never met and gently asks questions instead of scolding, knowing organised groups build such personas.

"He sent another photo," Arohi said, holding up the phone across the café table. "Look, him with the kids at the orphanage."
Urmila looked. The man was handsome, the light perfect. "That's the fifth good-deed photo this month."
"He's just a good person."
"Can I ask something without you getting mad? How much have you sent so far?"
Arohi's smile faded. "Some. For his daughter's school fees. And the hospital."
"Did he ever mention a daughter before he needed money for her?"
Silence.
"I read about this. There are whole offices that build one perfect man. One writes the poems, one sends the photos, one handles the money. It's their job."
"So I'm an idiot."
"No. You're a kind person being worked on by a team. That's not a fair fight."
Arohi set the phone face down. "What do I even do?"
"Tonight we call the cybercrime helpline together. I'll be right there."

qa.q: How many good-deed photos had the man sent that month?
qa.a: That was the fifth good-deed photo this month.

qa.q: What might Urmila be feeling as she asks how much Arohi has sent?
qa.a: Urmila seems worried for Arohi, asking carefully "without you getting mad" and gently checking how much money has gone.

qa.q: What makes Urmila's plan for tonight helpful?
qa.a: Calling the cybercrime helpline together means Arohi won't face it alone and can act quickly, with support instead of blame.

qa.q: How does Arohi seem to see the man at first?
qa.a: Arohi sees him as simply a good person, which is exactly the image the good-deed photos were built to create.

grounding: Urmila notices a stream of perfect photos and money requests, gently asks questions and explains that such personas are built by organised teams, without blaming Arohi.
